name: Robotic Grasping and Manipulation Competition: Manufacturing Track
ability_definition: The ability to make precisely coordinated movements of the fingers of one or both hands to grasp, manipulate, or assemble very small objects.

task_realism.reasoning: The NIST Task Boards are modeled on real small-part assembly. Robots insert pegs, thread nuts, mesh gears, plug connectors, and route wires and belts, all with tight tolerances. These closely mirror the assembly work where human finger dexterity matters. The task boards are still stylized arrangements rather than actual product assemblies.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Evaluation is physical, autonomous, and time-limited, with judges scoring under published rules. That is a genuine test of manipulation under real-world physics and uncertainty. However, it runs in a controlled competition setting with known board designs and a limited range of part variation. It lacks the variability in lighting, part variance, fatigue, sustained throughput, and quality stakes found on production lines.

construct_coverage.reasoning: It covers grasping, fine insertion, threading, and handling of deformable parts like wires and belts. It does not require multi-fingered hands, so parallel-jaw grippers with compliant control can succeed without coordinated finger movements. In-hand repositioning by the fingers alone and coordinated bimanual finger manipulation of very small objects are not required. A central part of the finger-dexterity construct therefore goes unmeasured.

format_match.reasoning: Inputs are real physical components such as industrial connectors, fasteners, gears, and cables. Outputs are physically seated or assembled parts, scored for correct and full seating, which matches real work artifacts. It loses some points because the task board is a standardized test fixture rather than a real product, and points-based scoring abstracts away production quality criteria.

transferability_reasoning: RGMC Manufacturing Track is a physically grounded test of small-part assembly with tight tolerances, so its tasks and artifacts transfer well to the workplace demands of finger dexterity. Transfer is limited mainly because simple grippers can succeed without multi-finger coordination or in-hand repositioning, and because the controlled competition setting and stylized task boards differ from real production variability.
